title: How do you solve a pricing case from start to finish, with a fully worked example?
description: The complete pricing case guide: cost floor, value ceiling and competitor reference, worked through an EV fast-charging price, plus mistakes and practice.
hook: Pricing cases have no single right answer, which can feel unsettling. The way through is to build a range from three sides and then pick a point within it, with a reason. Here is that process worked through with numbers.
body:
In this guide

  • When you will meet this case
  • The structure, and the first question to ask
  • A fully worked example with real numbers
  • The mistakes that cost candidates this case
  • Phrases to use
  • Practice prompts with model answers

When you will meet this case

Setting or changing a price.

The structure

What is the goal: profit, market share, or getting in fast?
  • Floor: our costs
    • Variable cost per unit (stay above it, unless it is a deliberate loss leader)
    • Fixed costs and investment (recovered over expected volume)
  • Ceiling: value to the customer
    • Price of their next best option
    • Extra value we add (savings · more revenue for them)
  • Reference: the alternatives (sit above or below them?)
    • Competitor prices
    • Substitutes

Cost sets the floor, value to the customer sets the ceiling, and the alternatives tell you where to land in between. Then check the effect on your other products.

A fully worked example

The prompt: a company is opening fast electric-vehicle chargers on motorways. What should it charge per kWh? (The figures are illustrative.)

Step 1: the cost floor.

  • Electricity and grid fees: about 35p per kWh.
  • Equipment: a £100,000 charger lasting 5 years costs £20,000 a year. If it sells 400 kWh a day, that is about 146,000 kWh a year, so equipment costs about 14p per kWh.
  • Floor: roughly 49p per kWh. Below that, every charge loses money.

Step 2: the reference. Say rival fast chargers on the same roads charge around 75p.

Step 3: the value ceiling. A driver on a long trip values speed and reliability; the alternative is a slower charger and a longer stop. Some will pay a premium, but few will pay far above rivals.

Step 4: choose. A price around 70p undercuts rivals slightly while keeping a healthy margin above the 49p floor. A subscription (a monthly fee for a lower rate) can lock in frequent drivers.

Then check volume. The floor assumed 400 kWh a day. If utilisation is half that, equipment cost per kWh doubles to 28p and the floor rises to about 63p, which leaves little room. So the recommendation depends on location and utilisation.

The mistakes that cost candidates this case

  1. Using only one lens, usually cost-plus, and ignoring what customers would pay.
  2. Not stating the volume assumption behind the price.
  3. Copying rivals without knowing your own cost floor.
  4. Forgetting how the price affects the client's other products or channels.

Phrases to use

I'll build a range: our cost sets the floor, customer value sets the ceiling, and rivals tell us where to land.
The floor depends heavily on utilisation, so I'd like to test the price at two levels of demand.

Practise with these prompts

What price should a company charge for fast EV charging?

Show a model structure
  • Cost floor: Electricity, grid fees, equipment per kWh; Utilisation needed to break even
  • Customer value: Cost of charging at home vs on the road; Time saved, convenience
  • Competitors: Rivals' prices, subscriptions; Fuel cost per mile as a reference
  • Structure: Per kWh, per minute, subscription; Peak and off-peak

Where to start: Cost floor vs value ceiling: price sits between the two.

The trap: Copying rivals' prices without knowing your own cost and utilisation.

Should an electronics retailer introduce a price-match guarantee?

Show a model structure
  • Customer impact: Extra sales from confidence; Share of customers who would claim
  • Cost: Margin given up on matched sales; Admin to check claims
  • Competitor response: Rivals matching back, price war; Online-only rivals
  • Rules: Which rivals and products; In-store vs online

Where to start: Cost: how many sales would be matched, and at what discount.

The trap: Assuming only a few customers will claim.

Should a design-software company add a free plan?

Show a model structure
  • Acquisition: New users attracted; Conversion from free to paid
  • Cannibalisation: Paying users moving down; What the free plan leaves out
  • Costs: Hosting and support for free users; Fraud and abuse
  • Competition: Rivals' free plans; How customers choose a tool

Where to start: Conversion from free to paid vs paying users who downgrade.

The trap: Counting sign-ups as success.

Keep going

  • The framework on its own
  • The quick version: first question and trap
  • More practice prompts in this area

Test profit, not merely revenue

A subscription service has 10,000 customers paying £20 a month. Its variable servicing cost is £6 per customer per month, so monthly contribution is £140,000. Management wants to raise price to £24, a 20% increase. Some customers may cancel.

At the new price, contribution per surviving customer rises from £14 to £18. The business can therefore retain the original £140,000 contribution if it keeps approximately 7,778 customers (£140,000 divided by £18). That means it could lose roughly 22% of customers before monthly contribution falls below the starting level, provided servicing cost stays constant and there are no offsetting acquisition or retention effects.

This is not a forecast of customer behaviour. It is a break-even retention threshold that tells you what research to conduct. Segment customers by usage, willingness to pay and switching cost. A high-usage customer may tolerate a rise that a low-usage customer will not. Test a price change in one cohort if feasible, measuring cancellation, upgrades, complaints and support costs, rather than extrapolating a survey answer into actual behaviour.

A pricing recommendation should specify who pays what, when it changes, why customers will accept it, expected impact on contribution and the principal downside. A successful pricing case is an economic decision under uncertainty, not a list of pricing models.
